Task 3:
Divergence 1 — Black-Box Performance vs. Auditable Decisions
Network evidence: deep-reinforcement-learning (6 docs) and explainable-ai (5 docs) share exactly one bridge document — Explainable Deep Reinforcement Learning For Production Control (Theumer et al., 2022). Every other DRL paper in the corpus (Wang Zhiyuan, Shah, Bashyal, Zeng, Müller-Zhang) carries zero explainable-ai tag. Every other XAI paper (Wang & Chen, Mehdiyev, Morandini) carries zero deep-reinforcement-learning tag.
Reading the gap, not just the bridge: a single bridge out of 6×5=30 possible pairings means explainability and deep RL are effectively disjoint research communities in this literature — Theumer isn't evidence of a trend, it's the only data point. That's a stronger, more precise claim than "there's tension" — it's "there is currently one published attempt to reconcile these, anywhere in this corpus."
Trade-off the organization faces: every other DRL paper you could deploy today ships zero built-in auditability. If Theumer's approach doesn't generalize to your architecture, you're not choosing between a transparent and an opaque scheduler — you're choosing between an opaque scheduler with a body of results, or being the second published attempt at explainable MARL for production control.
Divergence 2 — Guaranteed Robustness vs. Adaptive Learning Under Uncertainty
Network evidence: uncertainty (6 docs) sits at the seam between two camps that never otherwise touch: robust-optimization + rolling (Wang 2017, Long 2020, Zhang 2023 — 3 mutual co-occurrences) versus deep-reinforcement-learning (1 co-occurrence, via An Uncertainty Involved Two-Stage Energy Optimization…, Wang Zhiyuan 2025). robust-optimization and deep-reinforcement-learning never co-occur in the same paper directly — uncertainty is the only concept that touches both neighborhoods.
What this sharpens: the earlier version of this divergence said "these are two paradigms." The network says something more specific — nobody has published a paper that combines robust-optimization guarantees with a DRL policy for the same problem. Wang Zhiyuan's paper handles uncertainty by learning around it (fuzzy c-means + SAC); Long/Zhang/Wang-2017 handle it by bounding it mathematically. The corpus offers zero hybrids.
Trade-off the organization faces: unchanged in substance, but now falsifiable — if you want both a bound and an adaptive policy, there is no published reference architecture in this 31-paper set to copy. You'd be building the hybrid, not selecting between two mature options.
Divergence 3 — Exact/Matheuristic Guarantees vs. Metaheuristic Flexibility
Network evidence: matheuristic (1 doc, Gomes 2021) connects to heat-treatment and multi-objective-optimization — but never to metaheuristic. Meanwhile metaheuristic (5 docs) is one of the best-connected concepts in the graph, touching furnace, explainable-ai, prediction-model, heat-treatment, simulation, green-scheduling. It's promiscuous; matheuristic is not.
Sharper reading: this isn't just "exact vs. approximate," it's that the exact/guaranteed camp (Benedikt's polynomial-time result, Gomes's matheuristic) is methodologically isolated — each is a one-off result that doesn't recombine with anything else in the corpus — while the metaheuristic camp is the connective tissue linking furnace scheduling to prediction, simulation, and even explainability (via Wang & Chen's GA-based XAI paper). The flexible-but-unguaranteed approaches are what the field is actually building on top of.
Trade-off the organization faces: the guaranteed methods are stronger individually but dead ends architecturally — you can't easily extend Benedikt's optimal-control formulation to the next furnace-adjacent problem the way you can bolt another metaheuristic onto an existing GA pipeline.
Divergence 4 (new, surfaced only by the corrected network) — Two Optimization Paradigms That Have Never Met
The concept network makes visible something the paper-level view hid: metaheuristic and deep-reinforcement-learning never co-occur in a single paper, anywhere in this corpus. They're both general-purpose search/optimization paradigms; both show up repeatedly (5 and 6 documents respectively); and they simply don't intersect. Grey wolf optimization, genetic algorithms, and simulated-annealing-style heuristics live in one cluster; SAC, DQN, and MARL live in another; nothing warm-starts an RL policy with a metaheuristic solution, and nothing uses RL to tune a metaheuristic's hyperparameters.
Trade-off the organization faces: this isn't a trade-off the literature has already made for you — it's a trade-off nobody in the sample has made at all. Metaheuristics are cheap to deploy, don't need training data, and are well-understood by plant engineers; DRL needs simulation infrastructure and offers no convergence guarantee but adapts online. An organization that wants "the best of both" is doing genuinely novel work, not selecting a proven hybrid.

Layer 2 splits into 2a and 2b. The first blueprint gave matheuristic/robust-optimization the whole guardrail job and left metaheuristics without a defined role. But the network showed metaheuristic is the best-connected concept in the corpus (5 documents, touching furnace, prediction, simulation, green-scheduling) while matheuristic is a methodological dead-end (1 document, no reuse). Giving metaheuristics their own sub-layer — refining Layer 2a's certified-feasible region against the Digital Twin's full-fidelity simulation, the same job Sobottka's GA-in-simulation paper already does at the furnace level — puts each technique where the network says it actually earns its keep, instead of treating "classical optimization" as one undifferentiated block.
The Layer 2b → 3 handoff is flagged as novel, not reused. This is the honest consequence of Divergence 4: metaheuristics and DRL never co-occur anywhere in this corpus. The first blueprint implied "combine best practices" was mostly assembly. It isn't, here — warm-starting a DRL policy from a metaheuristic solution, or using RL to adapt a metaheuristic's search parameters online, is something this organization would be the first to publish evidence for from this literature's perspective, not something it can adapt from a paper. Budget and timeline should reflect that.
The Layer 2a → 3 handoff, by contrast, has a working reference implementation. Wang Zhiyuan 2025 is not just "a DRL paper" — its two-stage structure (offline ALADIN-based optimization, then online SAC policy responding to what the offline stage couldn't fully resolve) is the Layer 2→3 boundary, already built and published. This is the one piece of the blueprint that's lowest-risk precisely because the network showed it's the sole bridge between the uncertainty/robust-optimization neighborhood and deep-reinforcement-learning.
The Layer 3 → 4 handoff carries a single-point-of-failure warning. Theumer 2022 is the only paper bridging deep-reinforcement-learning and explainable-ai. If Theumer's specific explanation technique doesn't transfer to whatever DRL architecture Layer 3 ends up using, there is no second corpus precedent to fall back on — the org should treat the XAI layer as its highest-uncertainty component, not assume it's a solved problem because one paper exists.
Ladle and forging need a Phase 0 that doesn't appear anywhere else in the blueprint. Layer 2a's guardrails come from robust-optimization/matheuristic papers — and there are none for ladle or forging (both isolated concepts, zero cross-references). For every other line, Layer 2a can be built by adapting a published bound. For these two, the organization has to generate its own uncertainty model and safety envelope from scratch before Layer 2a can exist at all — there's no shortcut this literature offers.

Summary
Proposes a polynomial-time scheduling algorithm, framed as an optimal control problem, to minimise the idle-period energy consumption of an industrial electric furnace, and demonstrates its efficiency on a real furnace application.
Develops a proactive scheduling method for a steel rolling process that accounts for stochastic machine breakdowns, controllable processing times and deterioration effects, balancing the robustness and stability of the resulting predictive schedule.
Combines time-series forecasting of job release times with robust optimisation to dynamically reschedule the steelmaking-continuous casting process under uncertainty in a hybrid flow shop setting.
Adapts explainable-AI techniques to interpret decisions made by genetic-algorithm-based job scheduling, using job scheduling examples to demonstrate how transparency can be added to evolutionary optimisation outputs.
Proposes a two-stage data-driven deep reinforcement learning framework for steel-plant energy optimisation: offline learning solves a nonconvex ALADIN-based model via a Soft Actor-Critic MDP formulation, while an online fuzzy c-means stage handles real-time supply/demand uncertainty.
A literature review assessing how transparent and explainable current AI-based planning and scheduling tools are, motivated by the need for AI systems to work synergistically and trustworthily alongside human operators.
Proposes a batch-scheduling method for heat-treatment furnaces that minimises energy consumption and tardiness while modelling processing-condition uncertainty with fuzzy logic.
Introduces a framework for generating multi-objective counterfactual explanations in job-shop scheduling by combining predictive process monitoring with NSGA-II-based multi-objective optimisation.
Applies deep reinforcement learning to schedule steel-plant production around electricity spot-market prices, exploiting demand-response opportunities to reduce energy costs.
Develops a digital-twin-based scheduling approach for parallel walking-beam reheating furnaces, enabling high-fidelity physical-virtual data fusion and real-time monitoring to support precise, optimal control decisions in steel production.
Uses a multi-agent system with strategic anticipation and virtual market structures to dynamically reallocate and reschedule off-spec steel coil products onto alternative orders within the hot rolling process.
Jointly optimises production scheduling and ladle dispatching in steelmaking plants under an integrated model aimed at reducing overall energy consumption.
Presents a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach to production planning and control that incorporates explainability techniques, aiming to improve user trust and reaction time to disturbances such as machine breakdowns.
Develops a genetic-algorithm-optimised back-propagation neural network to predict heat energy consumption per ton of steel billet in a rolling reheating furnace, achieving 94.7% accuracy versus 90.24% for a standard BP model.
Applies the grey wolf optimisation metaheuristic to the heating furnace scheduling problem in steel production.
Proposes a human-centric job-shop production planning and scheduling system grounded in Industry 5.0 principles, combining digital twin technology with digitalisation to help planners adapt to changing production conditions.
Jointly optimises reheating furnace scheduling and rolling plan generation in the hot rolling process as an integrated multi-objective problem, solved with an improved multi-stage multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to accelerate convergence to the Pareto front.
Proposes a data-driven, intelligent optimisation method for dynamically scheduling hot metal ladles at the ironmaking-steelmaking interface under one-ladle technology, aiming to improve overall interface efficiency.
Presents an IoT-based digital twin framework for steel production, applied as a case study to predict and optimise key rolling parameters (rolling force, tension) for cold-rolled strip production.
Combines large language models with reinforcement learning from human feedback to guide a deep reinforcement learning agent for job shop scheduling, incorporating a Kolmogorov–Arnold network for intelligent manufacturing applications.
Uses multi-agent deep reinforcement learning to coordinate demand response and energy management for heavy industries with discrete manufacturing systems, integrating production scheduling with energy-market participation.
Develops a multi-objective matheuristic for a no-wait flow shop heat-treatment line in the steel industry, jointly minimising total tardiness and energy costs.
Designs optimal online algorithms for green reheat furnace scheduling that account for a job deterioration effect and a maximum residence time constraint, aiming to reduce energy consumption under online (unknown-future) conditions.
Proposes a rolling-horizon scheduling algorithm, combined with by-product gas forecasting, to optimally manage a by-product gas supply system in iron- and steel-making under demand and supply uncertainty, controlling gas holder levels for energy savings.
A perspective piece comparing artificial intelligence and intelligence-augmentation approaches for process safety, arguing that AI should collaborate with rather than replace human operators, and outlining the risks of AI/IA use in process industries.
Studies modelling and optimisation of hot rolling scheduling to meet real-time adaptability and precision requirements arising from multiple product species and randomly changing batch orders in steel intelligent production.
Combines discrete-event simulation with a genetic-algorithm-based multi-criteria optimisation to schedule and batch jobs across parallel heat-treatment furnaces at a casting manufacturer, balancing throughput and energy efficiency.
Addresses a biobjective hot strip mill scheduling problem under uncertain rolling processing times, proposing robust optimisation models that jointly minimise penalty costs and the total starting time of rolling operations to reduce slab-reheating energy use.
Proposes an energy-efficient hybrid flow shop scheduling approach for forging operations that mixes continuous and intermittent processing modes, accounting for multiple time factors to reduce energy consumption.
Integrates Digital Twins with Deep-Q-Learning to enable live, integrated process planning and scheduling decisions for service-based smart manufacturing production.
Studies a green scheduling problem for identical parallel machines with release dates, delivery times and no-idle constraints, proposing both a mixed-integer linear program and a metaheuristic to minimise energy-related objectives.
